details: picklescan before 0.0.22 only considers standard pickle file extensions in the scope for its vulnerability scan. An attacker could craft a malicious model that uses Pickle and include a malicious pickle file with a non-standard file extension. Because the malicious pickle file inclusion is not considered as part of the scope of picklescan, the file would pass security checks and appear to be safe, when it could instead prove to be problematic.

A vulnerability in the GraphCypherQAChain class of langchain-ai/langchain-community version 0.2.5 allows for SQL injection through prompt injection. This vulnerability can lead to unauthorized data manipulation, data exfiltration, denial of service (DoS) by deleting all data, breaches in multi-tenant security environments, and data integrity issues. Attackers can create, update, or delete nodes and relationships without proper authorization, extract sensitive data, disrupt services, access data across different tenants, and compromise the integrity of the database.

descriptions.value:
The MISP Modules website component contains an information disclosure vulnerability in the external tools management interface. The /external_tools/list endpoint returned stored API keys (the api_key field) in its JSON response via the ExternalTools model serializer. Additionally, the browser-based edit form pre-populated the API key input field with the stored credential value, exposing it in the DOM.

The /external_tools/list endpoint is accessible without authentication (the regression tests verify the response for both authenticated and unauthenticated clients), meaning any network-reachable client could retrieve the API keys for all configured external tools. These keys are used by the server to authenticate submissions to external analysis or enrichment services, so their disclosure allows an attacker to impersonate the MISP instance or directly access those external services.

The vulnerability also affected the edit workflow: the change_config endpoint previously required the API key to be present and non-empty on every save, forcing the key to round-trip through the client. The browser JavaScript stored the key in a reactive state object and updated the in-memory tool list with the credential value, further increasing the window of exposure in client-side memory and network traffic.

Affected component: the website sub-application of MISP Modules, specifically the external_tools module (serializer in models.py, list endpoint, and the external_tools_index.html template). The impact is limited to confidentiality of the stored API keys; no integrity or availability impact on the MISP Modules website itself is indicated by the patch.

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [website] keep external tool API keys out of responses

patches.subject: fix: [website] keep external tool API keys out of responses

assumptions: The /external_tools/list endpoint is accessible without authentication based on regression tests that verify the response for both authenticated and unauthenticated clients; however, the README notes that management operations require ADMIN_PASSWORD, so the list endpoint's access control may vary by deployment configuration.
CVSS SC:H assumes the exposed API keys grant meaningful access to external services; the actual scope of access depends on the specific external tools configured and is not specified in the patch.
No specific product version or release boundary is identified in the patch; the affected version range is therefore marked as unspecified.

CAPEC-126 is the closest available pattern but is not a perfect match; the vulnerability is more precisely an API response information disclosure than a session hijacking. No CAPEC pattern specifically covers 'sensitive credential in API JSON response' without a session framing.
The commit references issue #816 but no reporter or finder is named in the patch metadata or commit message.

The 60-character maximum length validation for API keys is a new constraint introduced by the patch; it is unclear whether keys longer than 60 characters were previously valid, which could affect deployments with longer keys.
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix removes the api_key field from the ExternalTools.to_json() serializer so that /external_tools/list no longer returns credentials. The edit form is changed to a write-only pattern: the API key input starts empty, a blank or missing value on save retains the previously stored key, and a non-empty value replaces it. After a successful save the client clears the key field and does not propagate the credential into the in-memory tool list. Input validation is tightened to reject non-string or over-length key values. Server-side tool submissions continue to use the stored key from the database.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: models.py: removed the api_key entry from ExternalTools.to_json(). external_tools.py (change_config endpoint): replaced the nested if-chain that required tool_api_key to be present and non-empty with a flat validation loop for tool_id/tool_name/tool_url, added a type-and-length check (string, max 60 chars) for tool_api_key when present, and made the field optional (write-only semantics). external_tools_core.py (change_config_core): changed tool.api_key assignment to be conditional on a truthy request_json.get('tool_api_key'). external_tools_index.html: initialized the form key field to empty string instead of tool.api_key, added placeholder and helper text, fixed a bug where the error-clearing selector referenced the wrong field, moved browser-state updates to after a successful HTTP response (res.ok check), and cleared the key input after save. README.md: documented the write-only key behavior. Tests: added browser-level (Playwright) and unit-level regression tests verifying the list endpoint omits api_key,空
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: the /external_tools/list endpoint is reachable over the network via HTTP. AC:L: exploitation requires only a single GET request with no special conditions. AT:N: no attack prerequisites such as race conditions or specific timing. PR:N: regression tests confirm the endpoint returns 200 and previously included api_key for both authenticated and unauthenticated clients, indicating no privilege is required. UI:N: no victim interaction is needed; the attacker simply reads the response. VC:H: the exposed data is API keys (credentials) for external services, representing high confidentiality loss. VI:N and VA:N: no integrity or availability impact on the MISP Modules website. SC:H: the stolen API keys can be used to authenticate to external analysis/enrichment services, representing high confidentiality impact on a subsequent component. SI:N and SA:N: no integrity or availability impact on subsequent components is indicated.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The /external_tools/list endpoint returned stored API keys in its JSON response to any client (authenticated or not), exposing credentials to unauthorized parties. The browser form also pre-populated the key in the DOM.

API keys used to authenticate to external services were stored and transmitted without adequate protection: they appeared in API responses and in client-side form state, violating the principle that credentials should be write-only from the client perspective.

capecRationale.rationale: The closest available CAPEC pattern. The attack involves an attacker obtaining credential material (API keys) from a web application response and using it to authenticate to a subsequent service. CAPEC-126 covers the theft of session/credential tokens from a web application. The mapping is imperfect because the keys are long-lived API credentials rather than short-lived session tokens, and the attack does not involve a session per se, but the underlying mechanism (reading a credential from an HTTP response and replaying it) is the same class of attack. No CAPEC pattern specifically covers 'sensitive data in API response' without a session-hijacking framing, so this is the best available match.

notes.text:
FreeRDP is a free implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), released under the Apache license. The xfreerdp client can connect to RDP servers such as Microsoft Windows machines, xrdp, and VirtualBox.

Security Fix(es):

* freerdp: FreeRDP: Denial of Service via uninitialized progressive tile handling (CVE-2026-109242)

* freerdp: FreeRDP 3.0.0-beta1 before 3.32.0 Use-After-Free via Smartcard Connect (CVE-2026-109676)

* freerdp: FreeRDP: Unauthenticated keystroke injection via premature input dispatch (CVE-2026-110838)

* freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via file descriptor exhaustion in serial device handling (CVE-2026-110830)

* freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via heap-based buffer overflow during MP3 audio decoding (CVE-2026-110837)

* freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via unbounded memory consumption during RDPDR reassembly (CVE-2026-110833)

* freerdp: FreeRDP: Denial of Service via grayscale JPEG clipboard conversion (CVE-2026-110839)

* freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via memory exhaustion in NLA frame parser (CVE-2026-111378)

* freerdp: FreeRDP: Arbitrary code execution via crafted persistent cache file (CVE-2026-111379)

* freerdp: freerdp: Arbitrary code execution via crafted persistent cache file (CVE-2026-111381)

* freerdp: freerdp: Arbitrary code execution via crafted display frames (CVE-2026-111382)

* freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via heap out-of-bounds write in NTLM authentication (CVE-2026-111880)

* freerdp: FreeRDP: heap buffer overflow in server rdpsnd via crafted audio formats (CVE-2026-114045)

Bug Fix(es) and Enhancement(s):

* Rebase FreeRDP to 3.32.2 or newer [rhel-10.2.z] (JIRA:RHEL-277442)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A malicious Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server can exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted sequence of progressive display tile updates to a connecting client. Because decompression buffers are allocated without being initialized, processing these updates can trigger an internal assertion failure that terminates the client application or causes uninitialized heap memory to be rendered directly onto the screen. This allows an attacker to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) or disclose sensitive information.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: FreeRDP: Denial of Service via uninitialized progressive tile handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important rather than Moderate because a compromised or malicious remote desktop endpoint can trigger an unhandled crash or leak uninitialized process memory to the client display without requiring privileges. In Red Hat Enterprise Linux, FreeRDP packages are primarily utilized to establish outbound remote desktop sessions, meaning exposure depends on connecting to an untrusted server. While the attack occurs over the network, exploitation relies on user interaction to initiate the connection to a rogue host rather than exposing a continuously listening network service.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. When a user connects to a malicious Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server, the server can trigger an invalid smartcard connect operation, leading to a use-after-free vulnerability where previously released memory is accessed. A remote attacker can exploit this issue to cause memory corruption, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution or a Denial of Service (DoS) through an application crash.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: FreeRDP 3.0.0-beta1 before 3.32.0 Use-After-Free via Smartcard Connect
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This flaw is rated Important because a malicious RDP peer can trigger memory corruption in the FreeRDP client after the user connects (UI:R), with potential impact beyond a simple crash. Red Hat heap/allocator hardening and ASLR raise exploitation difficulty but do not justify lowering Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability in the base score when corruption is confirmed. This is the highest-severity issue in this FreeRDP set (CVSS 8.8) but remains Important rather than Critical because exploitation requires the user to connect to a malicious RDP server (UI:R).

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A malicious Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server can trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending repeated serial device creation requests when serial port redirection is enabled. Because FreeRDP fails to release previous communication handles before allocating new ones, the client application exhausts available file descriptors and terminates unexpectedly.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via file descriptor exhaustion in serial device handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated Moderate for Red Hat Enterprise Linux because the impact is confined to client-side denial of service and requires an explicit, non-default feature configuration. FreeRDP does not enable serial device redirection by default, meaning an attacker-controlled RDP server can only trigger descriptor exhaustion if the client session specifically opted into serial forwarding. Additionally, the flaw affects only availability without impacting system confidentiality or data integrity.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. The proxy component fails to enforce cumulative or absolute size limits when reassembling Remote Desktop Protocol Device Redirection (RDPDR) channel fragments. A remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by transmitting an initial fragment followed by continuous data fragments without a termination marker, causing unbounded memory retention in the proxy session. This excessive memory consumption can ultimately lead to a Denial of Service (DoS).
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via unbounded memory consumption during RDPDR reassembly
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Moderate severity because exploitation requires an established session with device redirection and a proxy explicitly configured to intercept RDPDR channel traffic, resulting in resource exhaustion without compromising data integrity, confidentiality, or allowing arbitrary code execution. In standard Red Hat deployments, FreeRDP is predominantly utilized as a client application or library rather than an intermediary proxy service. Consequently, typical environments are not exposed to this issue unless the proxy is actively deployed with channel interception enabled. Furthermore, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and 9 are unaffected because they provide earlier FreeRDP versions lacking the vulnerable proxy code.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A malicious Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server can exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted MP3 audio data to a connected client. Due to an incorrect buffer size calculation during audio decoding, decoded audio data can be written beyond allocated memory limits, resulting in a heap-based buffer overflow. This flaw allows an attacker to crash the client application, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).

notes.text: This flaw is rated Important because crafted MP3 audio from a malicious RDP server can cause a heap buffer overflow in the client after the user connects (UI:R), with integrity and availability impact and limited confidentiality impact (CVSS 7.1). Decode-path constraints keep Attack Complexity High. Allocator hardening may impede exploitation but does not clear I:H/A:H.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this issue by connecting to the shadow server and transmitting input data before authentication is completed. This allows the attacker to inject synthetic keystrokes directly into the host user's active session, potentially performing unauthorized actions on the host system.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: FreeRDP: Unauthenticated keystroke injection via premature input dispatch
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: Red Hat has rated this vulnerability as Important because an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access to a running shadow server can bypass authentication checks and inject synthetic keystrokes directly into an active graphical session. This issue specifically affects environments using FreeRDP 3, which is included in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, whereas earlier enterprise versions utilizing FreeRDP 2 do not contain the vulnerable state-machine code. Overall exposure is limited on standard systems because the FreeRDP shadow daemon is not active by default and requires explicit execution by an administrator or user.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. This vulnerability allows a local attacker to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (DoS) by supplying a specially crafted persistent cache file. When processing the malformed cache file, an arithmetic calculation error causes an undersized memory buffer to be allocated, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow during data read operations.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: FreeRDP: Arbitrary code execution via crafted persistent cache file
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: An important-severity heap-based buffer overflow was found in FreeRDP's persistent bitmap cache handling. When FreeRDP loads a persistent cache file, an integer wraparound in the size calculation in persist_cache_get_data, triggered by large attacker-controlled width and height values in a crafted v3 persistent cache file, causes an undersized buffer to be allocated, which is then overflowed when the entry is read in persistent_cache_read_entry_v3. A local attacker who can place a crafted persistent cache file and have it loaded by a user could use this flaw to crash the FreeRDP client or potentially execute arbitrary code in the context of the client process. The freerdp component is affected as shipped in multiple Red Hat Enterprise Linux versions, in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS, and in the Fedora and EPEL community streams, where a fix is being pursued; the Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 Extended Lifecycle Support stream is out of support scope. Red Hat rates this flaw as IMPORTANT with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.3, consistent with the upstream severity assessment.

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Arbitrary code execution via crafted persistent cache file
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: A heap-based buffer overflow was found in FreeRDP's persistent cache v2 parser (persistent_cache_read_entry_v2 in libfreerdp/cache/persistent.c). An integer wraparound in the bitmap size calculation allows a crafted persistent cache v2 file containing oversized width and height values to bypass bounds checks, causing mismatched entry size accounting and fixed 16 KiB reads that corrupt heap memory. A local attacker can exploit this flaw by convincing a user to load a maliciously crafted persistent cache file, resulting in a crash of the FreeRDP client or potential arbitrary code execution in the context of the user running the client. Red Hat rates this flaw as IMPORTANT (CVSS 7.3, CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), consistent with the upstream Important rating, with exploitation requiring user interaction to load the attacker-supplied cache file. The freerdp package as shipped in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10, freerdp and freerdp2 in Red Hat In-Vehicle OS, and freerdp and freerdp2 in Fedora and EPEL are affected, and fixes for these products are being pursued.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. An out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the server-side NT LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication path can result in a Denial of Service (DoS). When processing authentication messages with hash callbacks enabled, FreeRDP fails to properly validate the Message Integrity Check (MIC) offset. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this issue by sending a specially crafted authentication message, corrupting heap memory and causing the server to crash.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via heap out-of-bounds write in NTLM authentication
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This issue is reachable only on FreeRDP server or proxy peers that configure the non-default SspiNtlmHashCallback NTLM hash callback, which is reflected as Attack Complexity: High. An unauthenticated network attacker can cause a fixed 16-byte out-of-bounds heap write, so Integrity and Availability are High; Confidentiality is None. Red Hat rates this Important. Platform safeguards such as ASLR, NX, FORTIFY_SOURCE, and glibc allocator hardening may impede reliable code execution, but they do not prevent the out-of-bounds write or process crash, so the base metrics are unchanged.

Do not expose FreeRDP server or proxy endpoints that use SspiNtlmHashCallback to untrusted networks; restrict access with a host firewall and network segmentation. If the NTLM hash callback is not required, leave it unset so the vulnerable MIC path is not entered.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-10-20) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce bounds validation on Message Integrity Check (MIC) offsets within the authenticate message buffer before writing in ntlm_computeMicValue: upgrade to FreeRDP 3.32.0 (or the fixed Freerdp builds), which validate that the MIC offset is within the authenticate message buffer bounds before writing bytes, closing crafted NTLM AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE with backward session-key offset and out-of-bounds MIC offset. Until patched, this is a concern on FreeRDP server and proxy instances configured with the non-default SspiNtlmHashCallback setting, so leave SspiNtlmHashCallback unset if NTLM hash callbacks are not required, and restrict network access to FreeRDP endpoints from untrusted networks using firewalls and network segmentation. As a compensating measure, configure systemd service restart and watchdog settings to automatically restart FreeRDP upon process crashes and mitigate prolonged denial of service, require pre-authentication through a zero-trust gateway or identity-aware proxy before clients can reach the FreeRDP NTLM authentication handler, and restrict FreeRDP port access with host firewalls using firewalld or nftables to isolate the service from untrusted networks. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying heap out-of-bounds write defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-1311 Input Size and Quantity Bounds Enforcement (high)

Confirmed impacts include proxy process crash and potential heap content leakage to the backend. This Important rating aligns with the upstream High severity advisory rather than a Critical network-service compromise on a default Red Hat deployment.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the smartcard emulation feature where a smartcard context is released before its background worker thread is properly terminated. A malicious server can exploit this by sending a crafted sequence of smartcard I/O Request Packets (IRPs) to a client with smartcard redirection enabled. Successful exploitation can corrupt memory or cause the client application to crash, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS).
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via use-after-free in smartcard emulation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because an untrusted RDP server can remotely cause application crashes or heap corruption without requiring elevated privileges. The flaw affects client sessions where smartcard device redirection and emulation are actively configured, which is not engaged during standard RDP connections. In typical environments where smartcard forwarding is unused, client systems remain unaffected by this issue.
notes.title: Statement

notes.text: The CVSS score(s) listed for this vulnerability do not reflect the associated product's status, and are included for informational purposes to better understand the severity of this vulnerability.

Do not enable smartcard redirection when establishing FreeRDP sessions.

Ensure client connection profiles and command-line invocations omit the `/smartcard` parameter (for example, launch connections using `xfreerdp /v:<server_address>` without the `/smartcard` switch). In graphical connection managers or RDP configuration files, disable smartcard forwarding. Additionally, only establish RDP sessions to trusted endpoints.

Caveats: Omitting smartcard redirection prevents the use of smartcard hardware tokens and smartcard-based authentication within the remote session.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to cancel and join the background worker thread prior to freeing the emulated SCardContext in FreeRDP smartcard emulation: upgrade to FreeRDP 3.32.2+ (or the fixed Freerdp builds), which cancel and join the background worker thread before freeing the emulated SCardContext in Emulate_SCardReleaseContext, closing crafted sequence of smartcard IRPs containing ESTABLISHCONTEXT, long-timeout GETSTATUSCHANGE, and RELEASECONTEXT. Until patched, this is a concern on FreeRDP client sessions with smartcard redirection and smartcard emulation enabled, so Omit the /smartcard parameter from connection profiles and command-line invocations, disable smartcard forwarding in connection managers, and only establish RDP sessions to trusted endpoints. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying use-after-free defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A double-free memory vulnerability in the Kerberos authentication component allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause a Denial of Service (DoS). By sending a specially crafted Network Level Authentication (NLA) request, an attacker can corrupt server memory and cause the application process to crash.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via crafted Kerberos authentication request
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is evaluated with an Important severity rating because an unauthenticated remote attacker can trigger a denial of service or heap corruption across the network before establishing credentials. In Red Hat enterprise environments, FreeRDP packages are primarily utilized as client-side software rather than listening services, which significantly reduces the exposed attack surface on typical installations. Exploitation specifically requires an active FreeRDP server or proxy configured with Kerberos authentication, an associated keytab, and an enabled user-to-user negotiation mechanism, limiting the likelihood of widespread exposure.

Restrict network exposure by limiting incoming connections to trusted IP addresses or networks using `firewalld`, or disable the listening RDP service if remote desktop access is not required.

To restrict RDP access to a trusted subnet using `firewalld`:

```
firewall-cmd --permanent --remove-service=rdp
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=<trusted_ip_or_subnet>
firewall-cmd --reload
```

Warning: Reloading firewall rules may temporarily interrupt existing network sessions and will prevent incoming RDP connections originating from outside the designated trusted subnets.

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to ensure proper memory ownership or duplication of default Kerberos realm strings within the WinPR Kerberos SSPI retrieveSomeTgt routine during target principal assignment: upgrade to FreeRDP 3.32.2 (or the fixed Freerdp builds), which duplicate or properly manage ownership of the default Kerberos realm string when assigning it to a realm-less target principal, closing crafted NLA/CredSSP u2u TGT request containing an '@' in the server-name component. Until patched, this is only a concern on FreeRDP servers or proxies configured with Kerberos authentication and user-to-user negotiation — Client-only FreeRDP installations or servers without Kerberos and u2u negotiation enabled are unaffected — so Restrict incoming network connections to the RDP listening port to trusted IP addresses using firewall rules, or disable the listening RDP service and user-to-user negotiation. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying double-free defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. This vulnerability allows a remote attacker to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) or potentially execute arbitrary code on the client system. An attacker operating a malicious Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server, or acting in a man-in-the-middle position, can exploit this issue by sending specially crafted graphics pipeline commands. This occurs due to improper surface key truncation, causing an internal table to become inconsistent and triggering a heap-based buffer overflow when data is written past allocated memory boundaries.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: FreeRDP: Heap-based buffer overflow via surface key truncation in RDPGFX
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important severity because an untrusted or compromised remote desktop server can trigger heap memory corruption in the client process, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution or application crash. To exploit this flaw, a user must actively establish a remote desktop connection to a rogue server or have their traffic intercepted by a malicious intermediary. Red Hat Enterprise Linux systems acting purely as remote desktop servers or that do not initiate outbound connections to untrusted endpoints are not exposed to this issue.
notes.title: Statement

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to disable the RDPGFX dynamic virtual channel or restrict FreeRDP client sessions from connecting to untrusted RDP endpoints: upgrade to the fixed Freerdp builds, which apply the documented input check, closing all 3 injection vectors (malicious RDP server connection, man-in-the-middle RDP traffic interception, crafted RDPGFX pipeline commands). Until patched, this is a concern on FreeRDP clients initiating connections to untrusted RDP servers or over untrusted networks with RDPGFX enabled, so Restrict FreeRDP client connections to verified RDP endpoints, enforce network encryption against interception, and disable the RDPGFX dynamic virtual channel in client configurations. As a compensating measure, Randomize process memory layouts with ASLR to impede reliable arbitrary code execution, Enforce full RELRO and PIE to protect the Global Offset Table from overwrites during heap corruption exploitation, Enable Control Flow Integrity to validate indirect call targets and block control-flow hijacking, Deploy EDR agents to detect anomalous post-exploitation behaviors and child processes spawned by FreeRDP, and Enforce non-executable memory protections using the NX/XD bit to block execution of shellcode in heap pages. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying surface key truncation defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-101 ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) (medium)

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A malicious Remote Desktop (RD) Gateway or network attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a truncated WebSocket data frame followed by a Transport Layer Security (TLS) connection shutdown. Due to improper handling of the incomplete payload when the connection closes, the client enters an infinite loop, consuming excessive Central Processing Unit (CPU) resources until the application is terminated.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Denial of Service via infinite loop on truncated WebSocket frame
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having Moderate impact because exploitation requires a client to initiate a connection to a compromised or untrusted Remote Desktop Gateway, limiting the blast radius to client-side denial of service. In typical Red Hat Enterprise Linux environments, FreeRDP is used as an interactive client utility rather than a persistent background service. An untrusted gateway responding with an incomplete transport payload before terminating the secure session causes the client process to loop indefinitely and consume processor capacity, without threatening system data confidentiality or memory integrity.

notes.text: A flaw was found in FreeRDP. A compromised or malicious Remote Desktop (RD) Gateway server can send specially crafted Remote Procedure Call (RPC) network messages to a connecting client. Because the client verifies total buffer capacity instead of remaining buffer space before writing incoming data, client heap memory can be overwritten. An attacker can exploit this flaw to potentially execute arbitrary code or crash the client application, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: freerdp: freerdp: Arbitrary code execution via RD Gateway RPC client heap buffer overflow
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because successful exploitation enables a compromised Remote Desktop Gateway to corrupt heap memory and potentially achieve arbitrary code execution with the permissions of the client user. Exploitation requires user initiation by connecting through an untrusted gateway, preventing unauthenticated remote attackers from triggering the vulnerability independently. Furthermore, standard direct RDP connections that do not route traffic through RD Gateway RPC transport are not exposed to this flaw.
notes.title: Statement

https://access.redhat.com/articles/11258

Limit FreeRDP connections strictly to trusted Remote Desktop Gateways and ensure server certificate verification is enforced.

Operational controls:
1. Avoid routing RDP connections through untrusted or unverified RD Gateways (do not supply untrusted hosts to the `/g:` or `/gw:` parameters).
2. Connect directly to target RDP servers, utilizing a trusted VPN rather than an intermediate RD Gateway where feasible.
3. Ensure strict TLS certificate validation is maintained; do not supply the `/cert:ignore` option on the command line or disable certificate validation in connection profiles.

If FreeRDP client functionality is not required on the system, remove the package:
# dnf remove freerdp

Caveats: Removing the `freerdp` package may also remove dependent desktop packages or graphical remote desktop clients (such as GNOME Connections or Remmina).

--- CME Mitigation Guidance (2026-11-06) ---
Disclaimer: The following mitigation solutions are provided as a courtesy, pending the application of an official patch. This content was generated utilizing AI tools in conjunction with data from https://cmetaxonomy.org. Customers are advised to independently evaluate and test these temporary mitigations within their own infrastructure.

The highest-value action is to enforce remaining stream buffer capacity validation rather than total capacity checks in the FreeRDP RD Gateway RPC client during fragment processing: upgrade to FreeRDP 3.32.2 (or the fixed Freerdp builds), which verify remaining buffer capacity from the current stream offset instead of total capacity before writing incoming RPC fragments, closing all 2 injection vectors (crafted RPC BIND_ACK fragments, crafted RPC ALTER_CONTEXT_RESP fragments). Until patched, this is only a concern on FreeRDP client connections routed through an RD Gateway — Direct RDP connections not routed through RD Gateway RPC transport are unaffected — so Avoid routing RDP connections through untrusted RD Gateways, connect directly over trusted VPNs instead of intermediate gateways, and maintain strict TLS certificate validation by avoiding cert:ignore options. As a compensating measure, Enable ASLR to randomize FreeRDP memory addresses and complicate reliable exploitation following heap corruption, Enforce Full RELRO and PIE to prevent Global Offset Table overwrites and randomize code segment locations, Use Control Flow Integrity or Shadow Call Stack to validate indirect call targets against function pointer hijacking, Deploy EDR agents to monitor and detect anomalous process execution or memory injection spawned from the FreeRDP process, and Enforce NX/XD non-executable memory protections on the heap to prevent execution of injected payload code. These controls limit blast radius and contain exploitation, but they do not fix the underlying heap-based buffer overflow defect — apply the upstream patch to fully remediate.

Highest-impact CME: CME-404 Certificate Pinning (high)

An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. A remote attacker can forge authentication tokens and bypass security controls by signing tokens with an empty key. When verifying tokens against a JSON Web Key (JWK) set that contains an empty Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key, the library fails to enforce key-length validation. This allows an attacker to generate valid tokens carrying arbitrary claims to gain unauthorized access.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having an Important impact for Red Hat products because successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate forged tokens with arbitrary administrative claims, completely bypassing authentication controls. The flaw is not classified as Critical because exploitation requires a specific misconfiguration prerequisite—the target environment must actively load a symmetric key set containing a blank key entry. Typical deployments running standard authentication configurations are not exposed unless an empty HMAC key definition is explicitly ingested by the application.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When retrieving cryptographic keys from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint, PyJWKClient fails to validate HTTP redirect destinations against trusted domain boundaries. A remote attacker who can influence the response of a trusted endpoint can redirect key requests to an untrusted server, allowing the client to accept forged verification keys or potentially exposing sensitive credentials.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important impact because improper handling of HTTP redirects during dynamic key retrieval can allow an adversary to supply forged cryptographic keys or intercept sensitive request headers. In Red Hat environments where services utilize PyJWKClient to fetch JSON Web Key Sets over the network, accepting untrusted key material may compromise token validation and authentication boundaries. Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. The library fails to identify asymmetric public keys supplied in Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) format, inadvertently treating the public data as a shared secret in Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) operations. If an application supports both asymmetric and symmetric signing algorithms, a remote attacker knowing the public key can exploit this flaw to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass access controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because an attacker can forge valid JSON Web Tokens and bypass authentication mechanisms if public cryptographic keys are mistakenly treated as shared secrets. Exploitation requires a specific application scenario where both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms are concurrently permitted during signature verification and public keys are provided in raw DER binary format. Typical Red Hat product integrations do not employ this vulnerable algorithm combination or key encoding by default, which restricts the overall attack surface in standard production environments.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. When verifying cryptographic keys, the raw JSON Web Key (JWK) parser fails to normalize Unicode byte-order marks (BOM). In mixed-algorithm verification environments, an attacker who knows the public key can supply a key prefixed with a byte-order mark, causing the system to misidentify the public key as a shared symmetric secret. This flaw allows an attacker to forge authenticated JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and bypass authentication controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because successful exploitation permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and forge valid tokens, though exploitation requires specific mixed-algorithm verification settings. In Red Hat environments, exposure is restricted to services that simultaneously allow both symmetric HMAC and asymmetric signature algorithms while parsing public keys that contain byte order marks. Workloads and services that enforce single-algorithm verification policies or utilize standard asymmetric key validation routines are not susceptible to this attack.

notes.text:
An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. A remote attacker can forge authentication tokens and bypass security controls by signing tokens with an empty key. When verifying tokens against a JSON Web Key (JWK) set that contains an empty Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key, the library fails to enforce key-length validation. This allows an attacker to generate valid tokens carrying arbitrary claims to gain unauthorized access.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having an Important impact for Red Hat products because successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate forged tokens with arbitrary administrative claims, completely bypassing authentication controls. The flaw is not classified as Critical because exploitation requires a specific misconfiguration prerequisite—the target environment must actively load a symmetric key set containing a blank key entry. Typical deployments running standard authentication configurations are not exposed unless an empty HMAC key definition is explicitly ingested by the application.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When retrieving cryptographic keys from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint, PyJWKClient fails to validate HTTP redirect destinations against trusted domain boundaries. A remote attacker who can influence the response of a trusted endpoint can redirect key requests to an untrusted server, allowing the client to accept forged verification keys or potentially exposing sensitive credentials.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important impact because improper handling of HTTP redirects during dynamic key retrieval can allow an adversary to supply forged cryptographic keys or intercept sensitive request headers. In Red Hat environments where services utilize PyJWKClient to fetch JSON Web Key Sets over the network, accepting untrusted key material may compromise token validation and authentication boundaries. Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. The library fails to identify asymmetric public keys supplied in Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) format, inadvertently treating the public data as a shared secret in Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) operations. If an application supports both asymmetric and symmetric signing algorithms, a remote attacker knowing the public key can exploit this flaw to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass access controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because an attacker can forge valid JSON Web Tokens and bypass authentication mechanisms if public cryptographic keys are mistakenly treated as shared secrets. Exploitation requires a specific application scenario where both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms are concurrently permitted during signature verification and public keys are provided in raw DER binary format. Typical Red Hat product integrations do not employ this vulnerable algorithm combination or key encoding by default, which restricts the overall attack surface in standard production environments.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. When verifying cryptographic keys, the raw JSON Web Key (JWK) parser fails to normalize Unicode byte-order marks (BOM). In mixed-algorithm verification environments, an attacker who knows the public key can supply a key prefixed with a byte-order mark, causing the system to misidentify the public key as a shared symmetric secret. This flaw allows an attacker to forge authenticated JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and bypass authentication controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because successful exploitation permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and forge valid tokens, though exploitation requires specific mixed-algorithm verification settings. In Red Hat environments, exposure is restricted to services that simultaneously allow both symmetric HMAC and asymmetric signature algorithms while parsing public keys that contain byte order marks. Workloads and services that enforce single-algorithm verification policies or utilize standard asymmetric key validation routines are not susceptible to this attack.

notes.text:
An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.0 Extended Update Support.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. The library fails to identify asymmetric public keys supplied in Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) format, inadvertently treating the public data as a shared secret in Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) operations. If an application supports both asymmetric and symmetric signing algorithms, a remote attacker knowing the public key can exploit this flaw to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass access controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because an attacker can forge valid JSON Web Tokens and bypass authentication mechanisms if public cryptographic keys are mistakenly treated as shared secrets. Exploitation requires a specific application scenario where both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms are concurrently permitted during signature verification and public keys are provided in raw DER binary format. Typical Red Hat product integrations do not employ this vulnerable algorithm combination or key encoding by default, which restricts the overall attack surface in standard production environments.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. When verifying cryptographic keys, the raw JSON Web Key (JWK) parser fails to normalize Unicode byte-order marks (BOM). In mixed-algorithm verification environments, an attacker who knows the public key can supply a key prefixed with a byte-order mark, causing the system to misidentify the public key as a shared symmetric secret. This flaw allows an attacker to forge authenticated JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and bypass authentication controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because successful exploitation permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and forge valid tokens, though exploitation requires specific mixed-algorithm verification settings. In Red Hat environments, exposure is restricted to services that simultaneously allow both symmetric HMAC and asymmetric signature algorithms while parsing public keys that contain byte order marks. Workloads and services that enforce single-algorithm verification policies or utilize standard asymmetric key validation routines are not susceptible to this attack.

notes.text:
An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.2 Update Services for SAP Solutions.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. A remote attacker can forge authentication tokens and bypass security controls by signing tokens with an empty key. When verifying tokens against a JSON Web Key (JWK) set that contains an empty Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key, the library fails to enforce key-length validation. This allows an attacker to generate valid tokens carrying arbitrary claims to gain unauthorized access.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having an Important impact for Red Hat products because successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate forged tokens with arbitrary administrative claims, completely bypassing authentication controls. The flaw is not classified as Critical because exploitation requires a specific misconfiguration prerequisite—the target environment must actively load a symmetric key set containing a blank key entry. Typical deployments running standard authentication configurations are not exposed unless an empty HMAC key definition is explicitly ingested by the application.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When retrieving cryptographic keys from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint, PyJWKClient fails to validate HTTP redirect destinations against trusted domain boundaries. A remote attacker who can influence the response of a trusted endpoint can redirect key requests to an untrusted server, allowing the client to accept forged verification keys or potentially exposing sensitive credentials.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important impact because improper handling of HTTP redirects during dynamic key retrieval can allow an adversary to supply forged cryptographic keys or intercept sensitive request headers. In Red Hat environments where services utilize PyJWKClient to fetch JSON Web Key Sets over the network, accepting untrusted key material may compromise token validation and authentication boundaries. Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. The library fails to identify asymmetric public keys supplied in Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) format, inadvertently treating the public data as a shared secret in Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) operations. If an application supports both asymmetric and symmetric signing algorithms, a remote attacker knowing the public key can exploit this flaw to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass access controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because an attacker can forge valid JSON Web Tokens and bypass authentication mechanisms if public cryptographic keys are mistakenly treated as shared secrets. Exploitation requires a specific application scenario where both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms are concurrently permitted during signature verification and public keys are provided in raw DER binary format. Typical Red Hat product integrations do not employ this vulnerable algorithm combination or key encoding by default, which restricts the overall attack surface in standard production environments.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. When verifying cryptographic keys, the raw JSON Web Key (JWK) parser fails to normalize Unicode byte-order marks (BOM). In mixed-algorithm verification environments, an attacker who knows the public key can supply a key prefixed with a byte-order mark, causing the system to misidentify the public key as a shared symmetric secret. This flaw allows an attacker to forge authenticated JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and bypass authentication controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because successful exploitation permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and forge valid tokens, though exploitation requires specific mixed-algorithm verification settings. In Red Hat environments, exposure is restricted to services that simultaneously allow both symmetric HMAC and asymmetric signature algorithms while parsing public keys that contain byte order marks. Workloads and services that enforce single-algorithm verification policies or utilize standard asymmetric key validation routines are not susceptible to this attack.

notes.text:
An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.4 Update Services for SAP Solutions.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. A remote attacker can forge authentication tokens and bypass security controls by signing tokens with an empty key. When verifying tokens against a JSON Web Key (JWK) set that contains an empty Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key, the library fails to enforce key-length validation. This allows an attacker to generate valid tokens carrying arbitrary claims to gain unauthorized access.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having an Important impact for Red Hat products because successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate forged tokens with arbitrary administrative claims, completely bypassing authentication controls. The flaw is not classified as Critical because exploitation requires a specific misconfiguration prerequisite—the target environment must actively load a symmetric key set containing a blank key entry. Typical deployments running standard authentication configurations are not exposed unless an empty HMAC key definition is explicitly ingested by the application.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When retrieving cryptographic keys from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint, PyJWKClient fails to validate HTTP redirect destinations against trusted domain boundaries. A remote attacker who can influence the response of a trusted endpoint can redirect key requests to an untrusted server, allowing the client to accept forged verification keys or potentially exposing sensitive credentials.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important impact because improper handling of HTTP redirects during dynamic key retrieval can allow an adversary to supply forged cryptographic keys or intercept sensitive request headers. In Red Hat environments where services utilize PyJWKClient to fetch JSON Web Key Sets over the network, accepting untrusted key material may compromise token validation and authentication boundaries. Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.

vulnerabilities.title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. The library fails to identify asymmetric public keys supplied in Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) format, inadvertently treating the public data as a shared secret in Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) operations. If an application supports both asymmetric and symmetric signing algorithms, a remote attacker knowing the public key can exploit this flaw to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass access controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Important because an attacker can forge valid JSON Web Tokens and bypass authentication mechanisms if public cryptographic keys are mistakenly treated as shared secrets. Exploitation requires a specific application scenario where both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms are concurrently permitted during signature verification and public keys are provided in raw DER binary format. Typical Red Hat product integrations do not employ this vulnerable algorithm combination or key encoding by default, which restricts the overall attack surface in standard production environments.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. When verifying cryptographic keys, the raw JSON Web Key (JWK) parser fails to normalize Unicode byte-order marks (BOM). In mixed-algorithm verification environments, an attacker who knows the public key can supply a key prefixed with a byte-order mark, causing the system to misidentify the public key as a shared symmetric secret. This flaw allows an attacker to forge authenticated JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and bypass authentication controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important severity because successful exploitation permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and forge valid tokens, though exploitation requires specific mixed-algorithm verification settings. In Red Hat environments, exposure is restricted to services that simultaneously allow both symmetric HMAC and asymmetric signature algorithms while parsing public keys that contain byte order marks. Workloads and services that enforce single-algorithm verification policies or utilize standard asymmetric key validation routines are not susceptible to this attack.

notes.text:
An update for fence-agents is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.6 Extended Update Support.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Critical. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
notes.title: Topic

notes.text:
The fence-agents packages provide a collection of scripts for handling remote power management for cluster devices. They allow failed or unreachable nodes to be forcibly restarted and removed from the cluster. 

Security Fix(es):

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance (CVE-2026-102266)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation (CVE-2026-102268)

* pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets (CVE-2026-102271)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects (CVE-2026-102267)

* pyjwt: pyjwt: Token forgery via improper Unicode byte-order mark handling (CVE-2026-102272)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

notes.text: A flaw was found in pyjwt. A remote attacker can forge authentication tokens and bypass security controls by signing tokens with an empty key. When verifying tokens against a JSON Web Key (JWK) set that contains an empty Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) key, the library fails to enforce key-length validation. This allows an attacker to generate valid tokens carrying arbitrary claims to gain unauthorized access.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Authentication bypass via empty HMAC key acceptance
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as having an Important impact for Red Hat products because successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to generate forged tokens with arbitrary administrative claims, completely bypassing authentication controls. The flaw is not classified as Critical because exploitation requires a specific misconfiguration prerequisite—the target environment must actively load a symmetric key set containing a blank key entry. Typical deployments running standard authentication configurations are not exposed unless an empty HMAC key definition is explicitly ingested by the application.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When retrieving cryptographic keys from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) endpoint, PyJWKClient fails to validate HTTP redirect destinations against trusted domain boundaries. A remote attacker who can influence the response of a trusted endpoint can redirect key requests to an untrusted server, allowing the client to accept forged verification keys or potentially exposing sensitive credentials.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as an Important impact because improper handling of HTTP redirects during dynamic key retrieval can allow an adversary to supply forged cryptographic keys or intercept sensitive request headers. In Red Hat environments where services utilize PyJWKClient to fetch JSON Web Key Sets over the network, accepting untrusted key material may compromise token validation and authentication boundaries. Exploitation requires the target service to dynamically resolve keys via HTTP and relies on an attacker's ability to manipulate responses returned by the configured key server.

notes.text: A flaw was found in PyJWT. When an application allows both symmetric and asymmetric signing algorithms, minor formatting variations in a public key can prevent the library from properly identifying it as an asymmetric key. Consequently, the library improperly treats the public key as a shared secret key, allowing a remote attacker to forge valid authentication tokens and bypass security controls.
notes.title: Vulnerability description

notes.text: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
notes.title: Vulnerability summary

notes.text: This vulnerability is rated as Critical severity for Red Hat products because an unauthenticated remote attacker could forge valid cryptographic tokens and bypass authentication checks without knowing the private signing key. Exploitation occurs when consuming applications configure token verification to accept both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms simultaneously, allowing an asymmetric public key to be mishandled as a symmetric secret. Deployments that strictly enforce a single algorithm type or validate tokens using JSON Web Key sets do not permit this algorithm confusion and remain unaffected.
